vision: Vigil is the trust layer for autonomous coding agents: a cockpit that makes an agent run observable while it happens and provable after it ends. It never accepts a claim it has not independently verified — every PASS is backed by bytes on disk, every destructive action passes a rail, and every report is rendered from Vigil's own recorded observations rather than the agent's prose. The road to v1.0 turns that promise from something that works on one engineer's laptop into something any operator can install, trust and prove: the finished work reaches main instead of rotting on branches, the evidence check inspects content rather than byte counts, no report asserts a check the code never performed, no gate can silently go unenforced, the budget guard actually stops the run, and the artifacts are safe to hand to an auditor.
north_star: A run that is reproducible, auditable and portable: any engineer can re-run the same plan on a clean machine, replay the recorded event stream, and reach the same verdict without trusting either the agent or the operator who ran it.

strategic_themes.name: Ship what is already built
strategic_themes.description: Three branches hold roughly 1,250 lines of finished, tested source that main has never seen, all touching the same four files. Finished-but-unmerged work is not an asset: it is a compounding liability whose conflict cost grows daily, and in the case of the unwired redactor it is actively dangerous because the capability looks complete while protecting nothing.

strategic_themes.name: Escape the author's machine
strategic_themes.description: DEFAULT_RAILS and the example config encode /Users/nick, the OmniRoute checkout, ports 20128/20219/20239 and a launchd label, and install is `npm link` from a Desktop checkout. Until defaults are neutral, a scaffold exists and the package is published, the tool has exactly one possible user.

strategic_themes.name: Make the trust claims literally true
strategic_themes.description: The differentiator is 'verdicts are evidence-checked, not trusted'. Today the check is existence plus non-zero bytes, maxBudgetUsd is accepted but never enforced, unreached gates vanish into an empty branch, and a re-run happily accepts stale evidence. Close every gap between the claim and the code.

strategic_themes.name: Survive the SDK and survive the author
strategic_themes.description: Unchecked `as unknown as {...}` casts against an exactly-pinned SDK, no CI, untested artifact and config layers, and a bus factor of one. Harden the boundary, test the integration, and make regressions fail before runtime rather than mid-deployment.

strategic_themes.name: First-class non-TTY operation
strategic_themes.description: --plain exists but auto-denies approvals and emits prose. CI and SSH consumers need structured versioned output, a machine-readable exit summary, and an approval channel that is not a TTY overlay.

strategic_themes.name: Runs as a managed corpus
strategic_themes.description: runs/ captures full tool inputs and outputs verbatim, is never pruned, and can contain secrets. Treat the run corpus as a first-class artifact with retention, resume, comparison and export rather than an ever-growing pile of JSONL.

strategic_themes.name: Serve environments Vigil did not anticipate
strategic_themes.description: One plan format, regex-only rails and two probe types encode the author's workflow. Adapter and extension seams let the valuable machinery — evidence checking, rails, reports — serve plans, policies and health checks Vigil did not invent.

target_audience.primary: The author/operator — a solo engineer running high-risk, multi-phase deployment and migration work through a Claude Code agent, who needs hard proof that each step actually happened rather than agent prose claiming it did.
secondary: AI-assisted engineering leads auditing what an autonomous coding agent did on a production-adjacent machine
Platform/DevOps engineers running gated validation plans in CI or over SSH via --plain and --json modes
Teams adopting the Claude Agent SDK who need observability, safety rails and cost visibility around agent runs
Reviewers/auditors who read run artifacts (events.jsonl, gates.json, cost.json, summary.json) after the fact without the TUI
target_audience.user_sophistication: Expert. Assumes familiarity with Claude Code, the Agent SDK, terminal TUIs, JSONL log analysis and authoring gated validation plans. Phases 1 and 5 deliberately lower this bar for installation and configuration without lowering it for plan authoring.
target_audience.adoption_blocker: A second user cannot run Vigil usefully without rewriting rails and config, because the defaults encode one machine's filesystem, ports and services — and cannot install it at all, because there is no license and no published package.

phases.name: Escape Velocity
phases.goal: Every completed spec is on main, and a second engineer can install Vigil, run `vigil init`, and get a safe, neutral, honest run on their own machine — where a PASS means the evidence was actually inspected, a gate that cannot be enforced fails at parse time, no report asserts a check that never ran, a budget cap actually stops the run, and the artifacts are safe to share.
success_criteria: Zero occurrences of `/Users/nick`, `OmniRoute`, `.omp` or author-specific ports in shipped default configuration
A clean-machine install to first successful gated run takes under 10 minutes with no manual config editing
A gate whose Capture artifact exists but contains the wrong content is recorded as FAIL
A run that exceeds maxBudgetUsd halts and exits non-zero
No raw secret appears in run artifacts across the redaction test corpus
Zero unmerged feature branches carrying completed specs; `git log main` contains the work from 001, 004 and 005
No capability is merged whose engine has zero call sites in the shipping path
A gate authored without an id fails loudly at parse time instead of silently producing no verdict
Every section of VALIDATION.md is derived from a recorded RunEvent — no hardcoded assertions remain
docs/ is tracked in git and `npm install` from a git URL yields a working `vigil` binary
phases.exit_gate: An external operator completes a full 3-phase validation plan run on a machine that has never seen the author's environment, using a clean clone with no source edits — and main carries every completed spec.

phases.name: Hardened Boundary
phases.goal: Regressions in SDK integration, rails, config or the event spine fail at typecheck or in CI rather than mid-run on a production-adjacent machine, the SDK version can be upgraded without fear, the safety rails resist deliberate evasion, and enforcement degrades loudly rather than silently when the agent stops honouring the output contract.
success_criteria: SDK messages are schema-validated at the boundary; malformed shapes raise a visible diagnostic instead of undefined values
Typecheck, test, build and coverage run on every push, and a deliberate regression fails the pipeline
Contract tests replay recorded SDK streams, allowing the exact version pin to be relaxed to a range
A documented corpus of shell-indirection bypass attempts is denied by the rail engine
RunStore, config and probe layers have direct test coverage
A 10,000-event run stays responsive and flushes completely on interrupt
Adding a RunEvent variant without handling it in the reducer fails `npm run typecheck`
A partial config file merges with lower-priority layers instead of silently resetting them to defaults
A plan that ends with unresolved gates emits a contract-noncompliance diagnostic and exits non-zero
An invalid CLI enum flag exits non-zero with the accepted values listed
phases.exit_gate: The SDK dependency is upgraded to a newer version with contract tests green and no source changes required beyond the schema layer.

phases.name: CI Native
phases.goal: Vigil is a first-class citizen in pipelines and over SSH: structured output for machines, an approval path without a TTY, reports for every run, and a run corpus that does not grow without bound.
success_criteria: `--json` emits a stable, versioned schema consumable by a CI step, validated against a committed JSON Schema
Approvals can be answered from outside the TUI and every decision is recorded
Retention policy bounds the size and age of runs/ without deleting failed runs
Every executed plan produces a report, including mid-phase and interrupted runs
gates.json distinguishes passed, failed, not_reached and evidence-downgraded gates
`vigil tail` stays byte-aligned through unicode output and exits when the run ends
A plan nested three or more levels below the plan root is discovered and runnable
phases.exit_gate: A CI pipeline runs a gated plan set end to end, gates its own outcome on Vigil's JSON summary, and requires no TTY at any point.

phases.name: Resume & Compare
phases.goal: Long multi-phase runs recover intelligently from failure without re-spending budget or trusting stale evidence, and the value locked in the run corpus is unlocked through comparison, diffing and shareable summaries.
success_criteria: A failed run resumes from the failing plan rather than restarting the whole set
Stale evidence from a prior attempt can never satisfy a gate on re-run
Two runs can be diffed by gate verdict, evidence hash and cost
A single self-contained file summarizes a run for a reviewer who has never installed Vigil
The Ink layer has snapshot coverage and the transcript is scrollable
phases.exit_gate: A deliberately failed 3-phase run is resumed to completion, and the resulting runs are diffed and exported without re-running any passed plan.

phases.name: Open Platform
phases.goal: Vigil is publicly installable, extensible beyond the one plan format and rail syntax it understands, and no longer dependent on a single author's attention or environment.
success_criteria: `npm i -g vigil` installs a working binary on a clean machine
A non-XML plan format can be gated through the same evidence, rail and report machinery
Users can supply rails, hooks and probes as modules without forking
External tools can consume the event stream through a documented, versioned API
Releases are tagged, changelogged and published automatically from a green pipeline
phases.exit_gate: An external contributor installs from npm, adds a custom rail and a custom plan adapter without modifying Vigil's source, and ships a change through the documented contribution process.

features.title: Neutral default rails with environment profiles
features.description: Replace DEFAULT_RAILS' author-specific content with a portable, generic deny/warn set (destructive git operations, pattern kills, home-directory deletion, agent-instruction file edits) that contains no absolute user paths, hostnames or ports. Move the OmniRoute-specific rails (warn-real-omp-config, warn-live-db, no-checkout-main's Desktop/OmniRoute path) into a shipped example profile under profiles/, loadable via config. Introduce path-token interpolation (${HOME}, ${planRoot}, ${cwd}) so rails can express machine-relative intent portably.
features.rationale: This is the single hardest adoption blocker. Five of seven default rails reference the author's machine; one silently fails to protect anyone else's repo because it hardcodes a Desktop/OmniRoute path. Without this, every other feature is invisible to every other user.
source_pain_points: DEFAULT_RAILS and vigil.config.example.json encode the author's personal OmniRoute environment
Environment-specific defaults make the tool effectively unusable by anyone else without rewriting rails and config

features.title: Content-aware evidence assertions with hash recording
features.description: Extend Capture targets from existence-plus-non-zero-bytes to declarative content assertions: minimum byte size, regex match, JSON-path existence or value comparison, and expected line count. Record a SHA-256 hash and byte size of every verified artifact into gates.json. A PASS whose assertion fails is downgraded to FAIL with the specific failing assertion injected back into the live session, reusing the existing evidence-downgrade path.
features.rationale: The product's core differentiator is that verdicts are evidence-checked rather than trusted, but the check is currently satisfied by any non-empty file. An agent that writes one byte of garbage to the Capture path passes the gate — the exact failure mode Vigil exists to prevent. Hashes also unlock run comparison in Phase 4.
source_pain_points: Evidence verification is existence + non-zero bytes only — a truncated or wrong-content artifact still passes
Validation reports written by the agent are self-graded
Agent prose is unverifiable: PASS claims are not backed by artifacts on disk
acceptance_criteria: The plan parser accepts assertion syntax on Capture lines covering at minimum: minBytes, matches (regex), jsonPath, and equals/contains for the resolved value
A Capture target with no assertion retains today's existence + non-zero-bytes semantics, so all existing fixture plans pass unchanged
A gate claiming PASS whose artifact exists but fails its regex assertion is recorded as FAIL in gates.json with a reason naming the assertion and the artifact path
The failing-assertion instruction is injected into the live session via the existing inject path and appears in events.jsonl
GateRecord.evidence entries gain sha256 and bytes fields, populated for every verified artifact including glob/brace expansions
Assertion evaluation is bounded: files above a configurable maxAssertBytes are streamed or rejected rather than read wholly into memory
Unit tests cover each assertion type passing and failing, plus malformed assertion syntax producing a parse-time error rather than a silent skip

features.title: Enforced budget and turn guards
features.description: Implement Vigil-side enforcement of maxBudgetUsd and maxTurns: track cumulative cost across plans in a run, emit a budget.warn RunEvent at configurable thresholds (default 75% and 90%), and hard-stop the run at 100% by interrupting the turn, writing a terminal budget.exceeded event and exiting non-zero. Surface remaining budget as a live header element in the cockpit and in --plain output.
features.rationale: maxBudgetUsd is accepted in config and handed to the SDK but never enforced locally, and cost is reported by the SDK rather than independently guarded. For a tool whose premise is walking away from an autonomous run, an unenforced spend cap is a direct financial risk.
source_pain_points: maxBudgetUsd is accepted in config and passed to the SDK, but there is no Vigil-side budget guard, warning or hard stop
Cost accounting is reported by the SDK, not independently verified; maxBudgetUsd is unenforced locally
acceptance_criteria: Cumulative run cost is accumulated from session.result events across all plans and persisted to cost.json as a run-level total
Crossing a warn threshold emits a budget.warn RunEvent exactly once per threshold and renders visibly in both the TUI header and --plain output
Reaching maxBudgetUsd interrupts the active turn, halts plan sequencing, writes a budget.exceeded event and exits with a distinct non-zero code
maxTurns is enforced with the same warn-then-stop semantics
When no maxBudgetUsd is configured, behaviour is unchanged and no budget events are emitted
A unit test drives synthetic session.result events past the cap and asserts the run halts before the next plan starts
The cockpit header shows spend against cap as an absolute and percentage value when a cap is set

user_stories.as_a: operator starting a long autonomous run and walking away
user_stories.i_want: a spend cap that actually stops the run
user_stories.so_that: a runaway loop cannot cost me hundreds of dollars overnight

user_stories.i_want: to see remaining budget live

features.title: Secret redaction in run artifacts
features.description: Redact secrets before they reach disk. Apply a configurable redaction pass to tool inputs/outputs and event payloads covering known token shapes (ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the configured authTokenEnv value, sk- prefixed keys, bearer headers, AWS keys, private key blocks, .env assignments) plus user-supplied redact patterns. Replace matches with a stable placeholder that preserves a hash prefix so distinct secrets remain distinguishable in an audit without being recoverable.
features.rationale: Tool artifacts store full inputs and outputs verbatim, and runs/ is never pruned. Every run that reads a .env or echoes a header writes a live credential to disk permanently — an audit trail that is itself a liability, which blocks sharing run artifacts with the auditors the product targets.
source_pain_points: Tool artifacts store full inputs and outputs verbatim: runs/ can contain secrets
Auth token read from an env var or plaintext config field — no keychain/secret-manager integration
acceptance_criteria: Redaction is applied in RunStore.append before any write, so events.jsonl, tools/*.txt, gates.json and cost.json are all covered by a single chokepoint
The resolved auth token value is redacted by exact match regardless of pattern coverage
Built-in patterns detect sk-* keys, Authorization/Bearer headers, AWS access key ids and secrets, PEM private key blocks, and KEY=value assignments for names matching /TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD|KEY/
config.redact accepts additional user regex patterns, validated at config load with a clear error on an invalid pattern
Redacted values render as [redacted:<8-char-hash>] so two different secrets remain distinguishable across a run
Redaction throughput is benchmarked and adds under 10% overhead on a synthetic 10k-event run
A test writes a fixture tool output containing each supported secret shape and asserts no raw secret survives to disk

user_stories.as_a: operator whose agent reads .env files during a run
user_stories.i_want: credentials scrubbed from run artifacts automatically
user_stories.so_that: my audit trail is not a permanent plaintext secret store

user_stories.as_a: engineering lead reviewing an agent run
user_stories.i_want: to share a runs/ directory with a colleague or auditor
user_stories.so_that: the evidence can be reviewed without leaking production credentials

features.title: Schema-validated SDK message boundary
features.description: Replace every `as unknown as {...}` cast in the session handlers with Zod schemas that parse incoming Claude Agent SDK messages (assistant/partial/result/rate_limit/tool_use/tool_result) at the boundary. Unknown or malformed shapes are surfaced as a typed `diagnostic` RunEvent naming the offending message type and failing path, and written to disk, rather than throwing deep inside a handler or silently yielding undefined. Parsing is permissive on unknown extra fields and strict on the fields Vigil actually reads.
features.rationale: The tool's entire observability claim rests on correctly reading SDK messages, yet every read goes through an unchecked cast against an exactly-pinned SDK version. A schema change today produces undefined tokens, missing verdicts and silently wrong cost accounting mid-run on a production-adjacent machine. This is the highest-severity technical risk in the repository and it blocks upgrading the SDK at all.
source_pain_points: Hard dependency on Claude Agent SDK message shapes; handlers cast through `as unknown as {...}` with no runtime validation and will break silently on SDK schema changes
No CI, so regressions in the TUI or SDK integration surface only at runtime
acceptance_criteria: Zero `as unknown as` casts remain in src/engine/session.ts, enforced by a test that greps the source
Every SDK message consumed by Vigil has a named Zod schema whose parse-failure path is unit-tested with a malformed fixture
A malformed message produces a `diagnostic` RunEvent containing the message type and the failing field path, is appended to events.jsonl, and does not abort the run
Unknown additional fields on an SDK message are tolerated without a diagnostic; missing required fields always produce one
Cost, token and rate-limit values are read only through validated schemas; a missing total_cost_usd yields an explicit unknown rather than NaN or 0
A recorded real-session message corpus parses with zero diagnostics

user_stories.as_a: operator running a long autonomous session
user_stories.i_want: malformed agent messages to surface as visible diagnostics instead of silent undefined values
user_stories.so_that: I can trust that a quiet cockpit means nothing went wrong rather than that parsing failed

user_stories.i_want: a validated boundary that tells me exactly which message shape changed
user_stories.so_that: I can upgrade without auditing every cast by hand

features.title: SDK contract fixtures and widened version range
features.description: Capture a corpus of real Claude Agent SDK message streams as committed JSONL fixtures and add contract tests that replay them through PlanSession against a stubbed SDK, asserting the resulting RunEvent sequence, gate verdicts and cost totals. features.title: Rail evaluation over resolved command semantics
features.description: Upgrade rails from regex matching on a flattened `<tool> <primary> <json input>` string to evaluation over a parsed shell command: tokenize the command, expand simple variable assignments, resolve quoting, and evaluate rails against each resolved argv plus the normalized absolute paths it touches. Flag known obfuscation vectors (base64 pipes into a shell, `eval`, `sh -c` with a constructed string) as a deny-by-default `unanalyzable` category, and keep the raw-regex path available for user rails that want it.
features.rationale: Rails are the only thing standing between the agent and the filesystem in the default `auto` mode, which runs with bypassPermissions. Today they can be defeated by `X=stash; git $X` or a base64 pipe, and they simultaneously produce false positives on innocent strings that merely mention a pattern. A safety control that is trivially bypassable is worse than none because it creates false confidence.
source_pain_points: Rails are regex over a flattened tool-input string: bypassable via shell indirection (variables, base64, aliases, eval) and prone to false positives
approvals auto/gates run with bypassPermissions — rails are the only gate on tool execution in the default mode
Destructive shell commands in a shared repo/worktree have real blast radius
acceptance_criteria: Bash commands are tokenized and simple variable indirection is resolved before rail evaluation; `X=stash; git $X` is denied by the git-stash rail
Paths in resolved arguments are normalized to absolute form before path rails are evaluated, so `../../` traversal and `~` expansion are matched
Commands containing eval, base64-to-shell pipes or `sh -c` with a non-literal argument are classified unanalyzable and denied by default, with the classification configurable
A documented false-positive corpus (commands merely mentioning rail keywords in strings, comments or filenames) produces zero denies
A documented bypass corpus of at least ten obfuscation attempts is denied, each covered by a test
Deny-wins-over-warn precedence and existing rail configuration syntax remain backward compatible

features.title: Rail lint and dry-run command
features.description: Add `vigil rails check` to validate the active rail set (compile every pattern, report unreachable or duplicate rails, flag patterns containing absolute user paths) and `vigil rails test '<command>'` to show which rails a candidate command would hit and the resulting verdict, without starting a session. features.title: Artifact, config and probe test coverage
features.description: Close the named testing gaps outside the pure logic: RunStore artifact tests (events.jsonl append ordering and JSON validity, tools/NNNN naming and collision behaviour, gates.json and cost.json shape, session.json round-trip), config tests (file discovery precedence, CLI override merging, unsetEnv and env building, base URL and token routing), and probe tests (HTTP and shell probes with regex expectation, timeout and failure paths) against a local stub server.

These are exactly the untested layers where a silent defect destroys the audit trail rather than announcing itself.

no probes tests
no config/env-building tests
no coverage reporting
Local Claude Code settings (plugins, hooks, skills, env overrides) leak into runs and make them irreproducible
acceptance_criteria: Every line written to events.jsonl is asserted to be valid standalone JSON parsing back to the originating RunEvent, in order, for a synthetic run of at least 200 events

features.title: Strict gate identity with loud parse-time failure
features.description: Close the silent-no-op path where a gate authored without an explicit `id` can never produce a detectable verdict. GATE_RE requires a literal `VG-` prefix while the parser's fallback id is `${tag}-${n}` (e.g. validation_gate-4), which can never match. Make gate identity a validated contract: either normalise fallback ids into the matchable namespace or reject an id-less gate at parse time with a message naming the file, line and offending gate.
features.rationale: A gate that silently cannot be verified is the worst possible failure mode for a tool whose entire premise is that claims are checked. The plan looks valid, the run looks clean, and the gate is simply never enforced — a false sense of coverage in exactly the document the operator relies on. It fails silently today with no warning anywhere in the event stream.

features.title: Exhaustive event spine and a genuinely pure reducer
features.description: Make the 18-variant RunEvent union exhaustive at compile time. features.rationale: The RunEvent union is the spine every other module depends on, and the UI silently drops variants it does not handle — an added event compiles clean, persists to disk, and is invisible in the cockpit. For a tool whose promise is that everything it observes is visible live, an event that reaches events.jsonl but never the operator's screen is precisely the failure the product exists to prevent. The purity violation also undermines the testability that makes the 18-case fold verifiable without a live SDK session.

features.title: Layered config resolution with provenance reporting
features.description: Replace first-file-wins config discovery, which silently drops lower-priority values and substitutes schema defaults for anything a partial file omits, with an explicit layered merge: defaults, then profile, then project config, then user config, then environment, then CLI flags. features.title: Verdict contract conformance suite and compliance telemetry
features.description: Harden the soft dependency at the heart of enforcement: the agent printing `VG-<id>: PASS|FAIL` in a parseable form. features.rationale: Enforcement rests entirely on output formatting that Vigil does not control. A model update or a verbose formatting habit degrades enforcement silently rather than loudly: gates simply never resolve, and the run looks uneventful. An abandoned remote branch named for exactly this work shows the need was already recognised. Detecting non-compliance loudly is what keeps the trust claim honest across model changes.

features.title: Correct incremental tail follower
features.description: Fix `vigil tail`, which tracks byte offsets against a UTF-16 decoded string. Because plainLine emits ▶ ✓ ✗ and reports write ✓/✗, any non-ASCII content permanently desynchronises the follower and corrupts every subsequent line. Replace whole-file polling with positioned reads from a byte offset, decode with a streaming decoder that tolerates multi-byte characters split across reads, and self-terminate on run.end.
features.rationale: tail is the designated tool for the CI and SSH audiences this phase targets, and it is broken by the tool's own output: Vigil's plain-mode log contains the exact glyphs that desynchronise it. It also re-reads the entire file every 500ms, so cost grows quadratically with run length, and it never exits, so scripted consumers hang forever waiting for a run that finished.

tail never self-terminates on run.end
acceptance_criteria: Tail reads from a byte offset via positioned reads and never re-reads previously consumed bytes

Following a 10,000-event file consumes O(new bytes) per poll, asserted by a read-volume benchmark rather than wall clock

features.title: Recursive plan discovery and tightened schemas
features.description: Remove the arbitrary two-level limit in plan discovery (phases/<dir>/<file>) in favour of bounded recursive discovery with a configurable root, depth cap and ignore patterns, and tighten permissive schemas — notably ProbeSchema, which currently accepts a probe with neither url nor command and therefore silently does nothing.
features.rationale: Plan layout is dictated by an implementation detail rather than by user need: a plan one directory deeper is simply not found, with no error explaining why. A probe with neither a url nor a command validates successfully and then never probes anything, which is the same silent-no-op class of defect as the id-less gate. Both must be resolved before pluggable plan adapters generalise discovery further.

dependency_graph.notes: Edges point from prerequisite to dependent. VG-030 is the new root of Phase 1: it lands the three finished branches so that VG-002, VG-003 and VG-007 are authored against one codebase instead of a fourth divergent one. Beyond it, VG-001, VG-003, VG-006, VG-007 and VG-013 remain the roots that unblock the widest downstream surface: VG-001 gates all portability and distribution work, VG-003 gates every hash-dependent capability in Phases 3 and 4, VG-006 gates the structured-output and consumer-API surface, VG-007 gates everything whose value depends on being enforced, and VG-013 gates the CI-native and analysis line. VG-031 and VG-032 are small but sit upstream of the verdict and report surfaces respectively, and VG-033 and VG-034 are cheap prerequisites that make CI, distribution and the consumer API trustworthy.

prioritization_summary.rationale: Must-haves are the features without which Vigil's stated promise is false, unusable or unshippable. Landing the integration debt (VG-030) is the single highest-leverage must-have on the roadmap because it ships ~1,250 lines of already-finished, already-green work whose value is currently zero and whose merge cost compounds daily — and because it is the gate that stops an unwired redactor from shipping false confidence. Alongside it sit the five in-flight Phase-1 specs that make the tool installable by anyone and make the evidence, budget and redaction guarantees real, plus three newly surfaced trust defects that directly contradict the product's own claims: a gate that cannot be enforced (VG-031), a report asserting a check that never runs (VG-032), and a repository whose requirements baseline is untracked and whose binary does not survive installation (VG-033). Phase 2 must-haves (VG-006/007/008) stop silent SDK breakage and unreviewed regressions on a bus-factor-of-one project; structured output (VG-013) is the prerequisite for the explicitly targeted CI audience; and public distribution (VG-024) is what lets any secondary audience reach the tool at all. Should-haves materially improve safety, correctness and recoverability but have viable manual workarounds — an operator can hand-audit rails, re-run from scratch, or prune runs/ manually — and this is where the durability defects live: reducer exhaustiveness (VG-034), flag validation (VG-035), config merging (VG-036), contract conformance (VG-037) and the tail follower (VG-038). Could-haves are leverage on work already done: analysis, export, TUI polish, discovery generalisation and the extension seams that broaden reach after the core is trustworthy. Won't-haves are explicit scope boundaries for a 1.7k-LOC single-author tool.

risks.risk: Finished, tested work rots on unmerged branches while main stands still — and the unwired redactor ships false confidence if merged as-is
risks.mitigation: VG-030 merges 001 and 004 immediately in dependency order, blocks 005 behind proof that store/session/cli actually call the redactor, prunes the stale branch, and institutes a seven-day branch-age cap plus a no-orphan-engine merge rule

risks.risk: SDK coupling via unchecked casts against an exactly-pinned version breaks silently on any upstream schema change
risks.mitigation: VG-006 replaces every cast with validated schemas that emit diagnostics; VG-008 adds recorded-stream contract tests and relaxes the pin behind them

risks.risk: Environment-specific defaults and the absence of a license keep the effective user count at one, invalidating every adoption assumption in the roadmap
risks.mitigation: VG-001 and VG-002 neutralize defaults and scaffold config in Phase 1; VG-024 licenses and publishes the package in Phase 5

risks.risk: The core trust claim is weaker than advertised — evidence checking is existence plus non-zero bytes, budget caps are unenforced, unreached gates disappear, and re-runs accept stale artifacts
risks.mitigation: VG-003 adds content assertions and hashes, VG-004 enforces budget and turn guards, VG-017 makes gate state explicit, VG-020 reconciles evidence on re-run

risks.risk: Rails are the only control on tool execution in the default bypassPermissions mode, yet are defeatable by trivial shell indirection — creating false confidence that is worse than no protection
risks.mitigation: VG-009 evaluates resolved command semantics and denies unanalyzable commands; VG-010 makes rail sets verifiable before a run; VG-026 allows organization-specific policy as code

risks.risk: Run artifacts capture inputs and outputs verbatim, can contain secrets, and are never pruned — a compliance and disk liability that grows with every run
risks.mitigation: VG-005 redacts secrets at write time; VG-015 adds retention, size caps and visible truncation; VG-022 applies redaction to everything exported

risks.risk: Bus factor of one with no CI, no issue tracker and dense single-line source: any interruption to the author's attention strands the project
risks.mitigation: VG-007 automates verification, VG-011 and VG-023 cover the untested artifact and UI layers, VG-024 adds CONTRIBUTING and automated releases so a second person can ship

risks.risk: Scope expansion into adapters, extensions and a consumer API fragments a 1.7k-LOC codebase before its core is trustworthy
risks.mitigation: All extensibility work is confined to Phase 5 and gated on the conformance suite and stubbed-SDK harness from Phases 2-3; VG-028 and VG-029 are recorded as explicit non-goals

risks.risk: The TUI is the largest untested surface and the operator's only live view; a layout or render regression surfaces only mid-run
risks.mitigation: VG-023 adds headless snapshot and interaction tests at three widths and removes the global stderr monkey-patch; VG-013 provides a non-TUI path that remains usable if rendering fails

risks.risk: Synchronous per-event disk writes throttle exactly the chatty, high-stakes runs where observability matters most
risks.mitigation: VG-012 introduces a buffered, backpressure-aware writer with guaranteed flush on exit, landing only after VG-011 makes artifact correctness testable

risks.risk: Silent no-op defects let Vigil report success for checks it never performed — an id-less gate produces no verdict, a hardcoded report section asserts a mock scan that does not exist, and a probe with neither url nor command validates and does nothing
risks.mitigation: VG-031 makes unenforceable gates a parse-time failure, VG-032 derives every report section from recorded events, VG-037 fails runs that end with unresolved gates, and VG-039 makes ProbeSchema a discriminated union

risks.risk: The requirements baseline lives outside version control and the packaged binary does not survive installation, so the project cannot be picked up, published or recovered
risks.mitigation: VG-033 tracks docs/, adds a prepare script, gitignores runs/, extends typecheck to tests and adds lint/format; VG-007 enforces it in CI and VG-024 carries it into the published package

sequencing_rationale: Sequencing optimizes for de-risking rather than delivery dates, matching a solo author with flexible time and no external deadline. Phase 1 now opens with the merge train (VG-030) because the dominant fact about this project is integration debt, not missing capability: three branches hold roughly 1,250 lines of finished, tested source that main has never seen, all touching the same four files, so every day of delay multiplies a three-way conflict and risks discarding QA effort already spent. Merging 001 alone removes the adoption blocker; merging 004 closes an unbounded-spend hole; 005 is deliberately held back until its redactor has call sites, because a merged-but-unwired redactor is worse than none — it grants confidence that runs/ is safe to share while tokens sit verbatim in tool artifacts. The rest of Phase 1 pairs the committed specs (002, 003) with three trust defects that contradict the product's own claims and are cheap to fix while the files are already open: a gate without an id that can never be verified, a VALIDATION.md section asserting a mock scan the code never performs, and a repository whose requirements baseline is untracked and whose binary breaks on install. Fixing these in Phase 1 matters because every later phase renders reports, replays events and publishes artifacts built on exactly these foundations. Phase 2 follows immediately rather than later because the highest-severity remaining risks — unchecked SDK casts against a frozen pin, no automation running the now-larger test suite, silently dropped event variants, silently discarded config layers, and enforcement that degrades without a sound when a model reformats its output — all compound with every feature added on top. Hardening the boundary and turning on CI before building breadth means later phases land on tested ground. Phase 3 turns the hardened core outward for pipelines and SSH, which is where the tail defect finally becomes load-bearing and where discovery and schema permissiveness stop being tolerable. Phase 4 mines the run corpus for resume and comparison, both of which depend on the evidence hashes from VG-003 and the config provenance from VG-036. Phase 5 opens the platform only once the core is trustworthy, because publishing extension seams over unverified foundations would harden the wrong contract permanently.
